arXiv:0911.3458v1 [nlin.SI] 18 Nov 2009

Multi-soliton, multi-positon, multi-negaton, and multi-periodic solutions of the coupled Volterra lattice equation

Hai-qiong Zhao Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Shanghai Jiao Tong University,    Zuo-nong Zhu Affiliation: 800 Dongchuan Road, Shanghai, 200240, P.R. China
15 November 2009
Abstract

This paper aims to find new explicit solutions including multi-soliton, multi-positon, multi-negaton, and multi-periodic for a coupled Volterra lattice system which is an integrable discrete version of the coupled KdV equation. The dynamical properties of these new solutions are discussed in detail.
PACS numbers: 05.45Yv, 04.30Nk, 04.20Jb

1 Introduction

As is well known, in recent years there has been an explosion of interest in the study of discrete integrable systems. This is due to the important role they play in mathematics and physics and to their many applications. The Volterra equation

d​Und​t+Un​(Un+1−Un−1)=0\frac{dU_{n}}{dt}+U_{n}(U_{n+1}-U_{n-1})=0 (1.1)

is an important lattice. It has been shown that the Volterra equation possesses all useful integrable properties. For example, it can be solved by the inverse scattering transform [1]; it has the Darboux transformation and various solutions [2]; it possesses infinitely many generalized symmetries and infinitely many integrals of motion [3]-[5]; it gives the KdV equation in the continuous limit. As we known, the topic on the relations between discrete integrable systems and KdV-type theories has attracted much researches [6]-[9]. Here we quote Morosi and Pizzocchero’s monograph [8]. In their paper, KdV theory including the infinitely many commuting vector fields, the conserved functions, the Lax pairs and the bi-Hamiltonian structure is recovered systematically through the continuous limit of the Kac-Moerbeke (KM) system. Aiming to get more insight on the relation between Volterra-type lattice and KdV-type equation, recently Lou et al [10] introduced a coupled Volterra system

a˙n+an​(an+1−an−1)−α​bn​(bn−1−bn+1)=0,b˙n+bn​(an+1−an−1)+an​(bn+1−bn−1)=0,\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{ll}\dot{a}_{n}+a_{n}(a_{n+1}-a_{n-1})-\alpha b_{n}(b_{n-1}-b_{n+1})=0,\\ \dot{b}_{n}+b_{n}(a_{n+1}-a_{n-1})+a_{n}(b_{n+1}-b_{n-1})=0,\end{array}

which yields the two-coupled KdV equation,

ut+6​α​v​vx+6​u​ux+ux​x​x=0,vt+6​v​ux+6​u​vx+vx​x​x=0,\begin{array}[]{ll}u_{t}+6\alpha vv_{x}+6uu_{x}+u_{xxx}=0,\\ v_{t}+6vu_{x}+6uv_{x}+v_{xxx}=0,\end{array} (1.5)

through the continuous limit

an=1+δ2​u​((n−2​t)​δ,13​δ3​t),bn=δ2​v​((n−2​t)​δ,13​δ3​t).\displaystyle a_{n}=1+\delta^{2}u((n-2t)\delta,\frac{1}{3}\delta^{3}t),\hskip 20.00003ptb_{n}=\delta^{2}v((n-2t)\delta,\frac{1}{3}\delta^{3}t). (1.6)

Equation (1.5) has some physical applications including the atmospheric dynamics, Bose-Einstein condensation and two-wave modes in a shallow stratified liquid [11]-[13]. As we known, finding explicit exact solutions for the discrete integrable systems is an important and difficult problem. In Ref.[10], by using a simple function expansion method, various explicit solutions to equation (1) such as solitary wave, positon, and complexiton have been given. The generalized symmetries, recursion operator, and integrability of coupled Volterra system (1) with α=−1\alpha=-1 were given [14].

We first remark here that under transformations −α​bn→bn\sqrt{-\alpha}b_{n}\rightarrow b_{n} (for the α<0\alpha<0 case), or α​bn→i​bn\sqrt{\alpha}b_{n}\rightarrow ib_{n} (for the α>0\alpha>0 case), equation (1) changes to

a˙n+an​(an+1−an−1)+bn​(bn−1−bn+1)=0,b˙n+bn​(an+1−an−1)+an​(bn+1−bn−1)=0.\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{ll}\dot{a}_{n}+a_{n}(a_{n+1}-a_{n-1})+b_{n}(b_{n-1}-b_{n+1})=0,\\ \dot{b}_{n}+b_{n}(a_{n+1}-a_{n-1})+a_{n}(b_{n+1}-b_{n-1})=0.\end{array}

Although various explicit solutions for equation(1) have been given, the more general multi-soliton, multi-positon, multi-negaton, and multi-periodic solutions have not been proposed. We think that these explicit solutions can not be given by using function expansion method. Since coupled Volterra system (1.2) yields coupled KdV system (1.3) in continuous limit, while the latter has many physical applications, we think that finding new explicit solutions to coupled Volterra system (1) are important. This paper is devoted to make an effort on this topic. We hope to find new explicit solutions by using the Darboux transformation. It should be remarked that Darboux transformation not only is a useful method of obtaining explicit solutions, but also has an important role in mechanics, physics and differential geometry [15]-[21]. In this paper, we first construct the Darboux transformation for the coupled Volterra system (1) by a special observation. And then, new explicit solutions for (1) including multi-soliton, multi-positon, multi-negaton, and multi-periodic are derived by using the Darboux transformation. We also analyze some dynamical properties for these new solutions.

2 Darboux transformation for the coupled Volterra system (1)

In this section, we will construct the Darboux transformation for the coupled Volterra system (1) by a special observation. We can see that the coupled Volterra system can be read off from the real and imaginary parts of the complex Volterra system

d​und​t+un​(un+1−un−1)=0,\frac{du_{n}}{dt}+u_{n}(u_{n+1}-u_{n-1})=0, (2.1)

where un=an+i​bnu_{n}=a_{n}+ib_{n}. We thus can write the Lax pair of coupled Volterra system (1):

ψn+1(1)=λ​ψn(1)+bn​ψn−1(2)−an​ψn−1(1),\psi^{(1)}_{n+1}=\lambda\psi^{(1)}_{n}+b_{n}\psi^{(2)}_{n-1}-a_{n}\psi^{(1)}_{n-1}, (2.2a)
ψn+1(2)=λ​ψn(2)−bn​ψn−1(1)−an​ψn−1(2),\psi^{(2)}_{n+1}=\lambda\psi^{(2)}_{n}-b_{n}\psi^{(1)}_{n-1}-a_{n}\psi^{(2)}_{n-1}, (2.2b)
d​ψn(1)d​t=bn​ψn(2)−an​ψn(1)+λ​an​ψn−1(1)−λ​bn​ψn−1(2),\frac{d\psi^{(1)}_{n}}{dt}=b_{n}\psi^{(2)}_{n}-a_{n}\psi^{(1)}_{n}+\lambda a_{n}\psi^{(1)}_{n-1}-\lambda b_{n}\psi^{(2)}_{n-1}, (2.2c)
d​ψn(2)d​t=−bn​ψn(1)−an​ψn(2)+λ​bn​ψn−1(1)+λ​an​ψn−1(2)\frac{d\psi^{(2)}_{n}}{dt}=-b_{n}\psi^{(1)}_{n}-a_{n}\psi^{(2)}_{n}+\lambda b_{n}\psi^{(1)}_{n-1}+\lambda a_{n}\psi^{(2)}_{n-1} (2.2d)

from the real and imaginary parts of the complex Lax pair of the Volterra system

ϕn+1+un​ϕn−1=λ​ϕn,\phi_{n+1}+u_{n}\phi_{n-1}=\lambda\phi_{n}, (2.3a)
d​ϕnd​t=−un​ϕn+λ​un​ϕn−1,\frac{d\phi_{n}}{dt}=-u_{n}\phi_{n}+\lambda u_{n}\phi_{n-1}, (2.3b)

where ϕ⁡(n,t)=ψ(1)​(n,t)+i​ψ(2)​(n,t)\phi(n,t)=\psi^{(1)}(n,t)+i\psi^{(2)}(n,t). Further, we point out that the NN-step Darboux transformation of the real Volterra lattice is applicable to the complex Volterra lattice.

3 Multi-soliton, multi-positon, multi-negaton, and multi-periodic solutions to the coupled Volterra system (1.5)

In this section, by using the Darboux transformation, we will construct explicit solutions for the coupled Volterra system (1). Obviously, equation (1.5) has a seed solution an=1,bn=0a_{n}=1,b_{n}=0, which is related to the spectral equation

ψ(i)n+1=λψ(i)n−ψ(i)n−1,i=1,2\psi^{(i)}_{n+1}=\lambda\psi^{(i)}_{n}-\psi^{(i)}_{n-1},\hskip 20.00003pti=1,2 (3.1a)
d​ψn(i)d​t=λψ(i)n−1−ψ(i)n,i=1,2.\frac{d\psi^{(i)}_{n}}{dt}=\lambda\psi^{(i)}_{n-1}-\psi^{(i)}_{n},\hskip 20.00003pti=1,2. (3.1b)

We solve this spectral equation as
(a) for 2<λ<+∞2<\lambda<+\infty or −∞<λ<−2-\infty<\lambda<-2 ,

ψ(i)n=c1(i)k−nek2​t+c2(i)knek−2​t,i=1,2,\psi^{(i)}_{n}=c_{1}^{(i)}k^{-n}e^{k^{2}t}+c_{2}^{(i)}k^{n}e^{k^{-2}t},\hskip 20.00003pti=1,2, (3.2)

where λ=k+1k\lambda=k+\frac{1}{k};
(b) for −2<λ<2-2<\lambda<2,

ψn(i)=et​cos⁡2​k[c1(i)cos(kn−tsin2k)+c2(i)sin(kn−tsin2k)],i=1,2,\psi^{(i)}_{n}=e^{t\cos 2k}[c_{1}^{(i)}\cos(kn-t\sin 2k)+c_{2}^{(i)}\sin(kn-t\sin 2k)],\hskip 20.00003pti=1,2, (3.3)

where λ=2​cos⁡(k)\lambda=2\cos(k);
(c)for λ=±2\lambda=\pm 2,

ψn(i)=(±1)n[c1(i)(n−2t)+c2(i)]et,i=1,2.\psi^{(i)}_{n}=(\pm 1)^{n}[c_{1}^{(i)}(n-2t)+c_{2}^{(i)}]e^{t},\hskip 20.00003pti=1,2. (3.4)

By using the Darboux transformation, we obtain the various explicit solutions to coupled Volterra system (1.5) including multi-soliton, multi-positon, multi-negaton, multi-periodic, soliton-periodic, soliton-rational, and periodic-rational solutions.

Example 3. In this example, we give the positon and negaton solutions. The term ”positon” and ”negaton” may be pursued back to the works of Matveev et al. [22]–[26]. The positon is usually given by the trigonometric functions. The positon has some important properties which differentiates it from the soliton. For example, it has a square singularity at certain point x0​(t)x_{0}(t), and has slow oscillating decay at infinity, and changes its form with time. The negaton is usually described by the hyperbolic functions. The nonsingular negaton possesses similar behaviour of the soliton-like. However, it is different from the soliton. It is not a translational solution and changes its form with time. Following the strategy outlined in [25], we can obtain the positon and negaton solutions for coupled Volterra system (1.5). We first note that the limit k2→k1k_{2}\rightarrow k_{1} leads to the following Taylor expansion of ψ2,n(1)\psi^{(1)}_{2,n} and ψ2,n(2)\psi^{(2)}_{2,n}:

ψ2,n(1)=ψ1,n(1)+∂ψ2,n(1)∂k2|k2=k1×(k2−k1)+O⁡((k2−k1)2),\psi^{(1)}_{2,n}=\psi^{(1)}_{1,n}+\frac{\partial\psi^{(1)}_{2,n}}{\partial k_{2}}|_{k_{2}=k_{1}}\times(k_{2}-k_{1})+O((k_{2}-k_{1})^{2}), (3.16a)
ψ2,n(2)=ψ1,n(2)+∂ψ2,n(2)∂k2|k2=k1×(k2−k1)+O⁡((k2−k1)2).\psi^{(2)}_{2,n}=\psi^{(2)}_{1,n}+\frac{\partial\psi^{(2)}_{2,n}}{\partial k_{2}}|_{k_{2}=k_{1}}\times(k_{2}-k_{1})+O((k_{2}-k_{1})^{2}). (3.16b)

Then we can rewrite Wnr​(2)W^{r}_{n}(2) and Wni​(2)W^{i}_{n}(2) as

Wnr​(2)=|∂ψ2,n−1(1)∂k2|k2=k1ψ1,n−1(1)∂ψ2,n−2(1)∂k2|k2=k1ψ1,n−2(1)|−|∂ψ2,n−1(2)∂k2|k2=k1ψ1,n−1(2)∂ψ2,n−2(2)∂k2|k2=k1ψ1,n−2(2)|W^{r}_{n}(2)=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial\psi^{(1)}_{2,n-1}}{\partial k_{2}}|_{k_{2}=k_{1}}&\psi^{(1)}_{1,n-1}\\ \frac{\partial\psi^{(1)}_{2,n-2}}{\partial k_{2}}|_{k_{2}=k_{1}}&\psi^{(1)}_{1,n-2}\end{vmatrix}-\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial\psi^{(2)}_{2,n-1}}{\partial k_{2}}|_{k_{2}=k_{1}}&\psi^{(2)}_{1,n-1}\\ \frac{\partial\psi^{(2)}_{2,n-2}}{\partial k_{2}}|_{k_{2}=k_{1}}&\psi^{(2)}_{1,n-2}\\ \end{vmatrix} (3.17a)
Wni​(2)=|∂ψ2,n−1(1)∂k2|k2=k1ψ1,n−1(2)∂ψ2,n−2(1)∂k2|k2=k1ψ1,n−2(2)|+|∂ψ2,n−1(2)∂k2|k2=k1ψ1,n−1(1)∂ψ2,n−2(2)∂k2|k2=k1ψ1,n−2(1)|W^{i}_{n}(2)=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial\psi^{(1)}_{2,n-1}}{\partial k_{2}}|_{k_{2}=k_{1}}&\psi^{(2)}_{1,n-1}\\ \frac{\partial\psi^{(1)}_{2,n-2}}{\partial k_{2}}|_{k_{2}=k_{1}}&\psi^{(2)}_{1,n-2}\end{vmatrix}+\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial\psi^{(2)}_{2,n-1}}{\partial k_{2}}|_{k_{2}=k_{1}}&\psi^{(1)}_{1,n-1}\\ \frac{\partial\psi^{(2)}_{2,n-2}}{\partial k_{2}}|_{k_{2}=k_{1}}&\psi^{(1)}_{1,n-2}\\ \end{vmatrix} (3.17b)

Taking ψ1,n(1)\psi_{1,n}^{(1)} and ψ1,n(2)\psi_{1,n}^{(2)} as equation (3.6) or equation (3.5), and using the 2-step Darboux transformation, we can obtain 1-positon and 1-negaton solutions, respectively. However, they are too long to write here. We now analyze the asymptotic behaviour for the positon. We first have

×(c22(1)​cos⁡(θ−k1)−c12(1)​sin⁡(θ−k1))−(c11(2)​cos⁡θ+c21(2)​sin⁡θ)\displaystyle\times(c_{22}^{(1)}\cos(\theta-k_{1})-c_{12}^{(1)}\sin(\theta-k_{1}))-(c_{11}^{(2)}\cos\theta+c_{21}^{(2)}\sin\theta)

where θ=k1​n−k1−t​sin⁡2​k1\theta=k_{1}n-k_{1}-t\sin 2k_{1}, η=n−1−2​t​cos⁡2​k1\eta=n-1-2t\cos 2k_{1}. And Wn(i)​(2)W_{n}^{(i)}(2) has a completely similar formula. Substituting Wn(r)​(2)W_{n}^{(r)}(2) and Wn(i)​(2)W_{n}^{(i)}(2) into equation (2.17), and by careful analysis, we obtain the following asymptotic behaviour of the 1-positon:

an​[2]\displaystyle a_{n}[2] =\displaystyle= 1−f1​(sin⁡θ,cos⁡θ,sin⁡2​θ,cos⁡2​θ)n,n⟶±∞\displaystyle 1-\frac{f_{1}(\sin\theta,\cos\theta,\sin 2\theta,\cos 2\theta)}{n},\hskip 20.00003ptn\longrightarrow\pm\infty (3.19a)
bn​[2]\displaystyle b_{n}[2] =\displaystyle= g1​(sin⁡θ,cos⁡θ,sin⁡2​θ,cos⁡2​θ)n,n⟶±∞,\displaystyle\frac{g_{1}(\sin\theta,\cos\theta,\sin 2\theta,\cos 2\theta)}{n},\hskip 20.00003ptn\longrightarrow\pm\infty, (3.19b)
an​[2]\displaystyle a_{n}[2] =\displaystyle= 1−f2​(sin⁡θ,cos⁡θ,sin⁡2​θ,cos⁡2​θ)t,t⟶±∞,\displaystyle 1-\frac{f_{2}(\sin\theta,\cos\theta,\sin 2\theta,\cos 2\theta)}{t},\hskip 20.00003ptt\longrightarrow\pm\infty, (3.19c)
bn​[2]\displaystyle b_{n}[2] =\displaystyle= g2​(sin⁡θ,cos⁡θ,sin⁡2​θ,cos⁡2​θ)t,t⟶±∞,\displaystyle\frac{g_{2}(\sin\theta,\cos\theta,\sin 2\theta,\cos 2\theta)}{t},\hskip 20.00003ptt\longrightarrow\pm\infty, (3.19d)

where fi,f_{i}, gi​(i=1,2)g_{i}(i=1,2) are two rational functions of variables. The asymptotic behaviour (3.19) yields the conclusion that the 1-positon of coupled Volterra equation has slow oscillating decay. We have seen that the singularity structures of positons are complicated. For example, the positon of the KdV equation is singular [22, 24]; the positon of the Toda lattice is ’weakly singular’—– singularity occurs only at some values of tt for every lattice site nn [25]; non-singular positons of the non-local KdV equation and the discrete sinh-Gordon equation have also been found. The analysis of the singularity structure of the 1-positon presented in this paper is difficult, since the formula of this positon is very complicated. By using the method of numerical analysis, for the random values of tt (e.g., t=−8.45,−2,0,1.39,6.78,20t=-8.45,-2,0,1.39,6.78,20), we do not find the singularity of this positon for every lattice site nn. We thus think this positon is non-singular. This conclusion is supported by the Fig. 5 which describes the evolutions of the positon ( with c11(1)=c21(1)=c11(2)=1,c21(2)=3;k1=2c_{11}^{(1)}=c_{21}^{(1)}=c_{11}^{(2)}=1,c_{21}^{(2)}=3;k_{1}=2). We also make the graphs of the negaton (with c11(1)=c21(1)=c11(2)=1,c21(2)=−1;k1=2c_{11}^{(1)}=c_{21}^{(1)}=c_{11}^{(2)}=1,c_{21}^{(2)}=-1;k_{1}=2). Obviously, this negaton is not a translational solution and changes its form with time. N-positon and N-negaton solutions can be derived through the limit k2​i→ki,i=1,2…Nk_{2i}\rightarrow k_{i},i=1,2...N and 2N-step Darboux transformations.

Finally, we remark here that for α>0\alpha>0 case, setting cj​1(1)→icj​1(1),j=1,2,c_{j1}^{(1)}\rightarrow ic_{j1}^{(1)},j=1,2, or cj​1(1)→icj​1(1),cj​2(1)→icj​2(1),j=1,2c_{j1}^{(1)}\rightarrow ic_{j1}^{(1)},c_{j2}^{(1)}\rightarrow ic_{j2}^{(1)},j=1,2, we can obtain corresponding 1-form and 2-form solutions to coupled Volterra system (1.5).

4 Conclusions

We have found new explicit solutions for a coupled Volterra system by using the Darboux transformation. These new solutions include multi-soliton, multi-positon, multi-negaton, multi-periodic, soliton-periodic, soliton-rational, and periodic-rational solutions. We have analyzed their dynamical properties. For example, the multi-periodic solutions are periodic in both space and time under proper conditions. In the 1-periodic and 2-periodic cases, the period of the space and time are given. The asymptotics of the positon is described. The positon obtained in this paper is a non-singular solution. We also have made plots for these new solutions. They can help one better understand their dynamical properties.
